short: Biomass Organs Control the Porosity of Their Pyrolyzed Carbo
title: Biomass Organs Control the Porosity of Their Pyrolyzed Carbon

lanes.label: Classical tools
lanes.sub: collapsed to one node per state

states.title: Hypothesis and design
states.head: High-surface-area carbon for supercapacitors normally needs corrosive chemical activating agents added to the precursor. Why carbons pyrolysed from different organs of the same plant differ in porosity has not been examined.
states.detail: Absorbed: w1 (HYP/need), w2 (HYP/gap), w3 (HYP/hypothesis), w4 (DES/base_system), w5 (DES/variable_sweep), w6 (DES/route), w7 (PRC/treatment), w8 (PRC/synthesis). Premises: Stems carry water and salts up from the root while leaves make photosynthate, so the ion load should be higher in the stem

states.title: Structure state
states.head: The stem carries more total metal than the leaf and about 2.5 wt% K against 0.9 wt%. The carbons inherit the organ architecture, the stem carbon keeping an interconnected network of 5-30 um transport channels.
states.detail: Absorbed: w9 (STR/chemistry/composition), w10 (STR/microstructure/shape), w11 (STR/microstructure/porosity), w12 (STR/microstructure/porosity), w16 (STR/microstructure/porosity)

states.title: Property state and mechanisms
states.head: Potassium held at molecular dispersion inside the tissue activates the carbon in situ during pyrolysis, cutting both micropores and mesopores. S-carbon gives 174 F/g at 5 mV/s in 6 M KOH against 152 F/g for L-carbon
states.detail: Absorbed: w13 (MEC/pathway), w14 (PRP/value). Premises: Alkalis naturally embedded in biomass activate the material during carbonization and create porosity in the carbon; Only part of the pore surface of a porous carbon is used for ion adsorption during charge and discharge

states.title: Performance state
states.head: The S-carbon symmetric cell keeps 72% of its capacitance at 500 mV/s and shows no fading over 10 000 cycles at 1 A/g

states.title: Conclusion
states.head: A plant organ's physiological ion load sets the porosity of its pyrolysed carbon, giving high-surface-area carbon with no added activating agent

nodes.title: TEM:STEM, F1, F3, F5, F6
nodes.head: Char residue at 800 C drops from 30.8% for the stem to 20.0% for the acid-washed stem, and the DTG's 200-310 C multiplet collapses into one sharp 330 C peak. Surface area climbs with pyrolysis temperature to 1610 m2/g at 800 C for S-carbon and then falls to 1580 at 900, while L-carbon keeps rising to 1290.
nodes.solves: Potassium held at molecular dispersion inside the tissue activates the carbon in situ during pyrolysis, cutting both micropores and mesopores

panel_conditions.condition: TGA and DTG curves of the stems and HCl-washed stems

nodes.note: residues also read at 500 C: 37.8% vs 24.8% bar heights read off F3d; the stem-over-leaf gap is widest at 800 C (1610 vs 1040) and has narrowed to 1580 vs 1290 by 900 C, which the text does not mention. Kept here rather than as an audit node of its own, since x9 is already the primary evidence for w13. judge re-read of the three ICP panels. Lotus F1e: Ca 0.72 (leaf) vs 0.50 (stem) and Mg 0.55 vs 0.21, but Na, Al, Fe and Cu are all HIGHER in the lotus stem. Celery F5d and asparagus lettuce F6d: every element except K (and Na, Cu, Zn in F6d) is higher in the leaf. So the leaf-over-stem inversion is consistent only for the alkaline earths Ca and Mg; the original 'Ca, Mg, Al and Fe in all three plants' was wrong for lotus. The audit's point stands: the paper's 'alkali or alkaline earth' framing of the activation holds only for the alkali.

Celery F5d and asparagus lettuce F6d: every element except K (and Na, Cu, Zn in F6d) is higher in the leaf. So the leaf-over-stem inversion is consistent only for the alkaline earths Ca and Mg; the original 'Ca, Mg, Al and Fe in all three plants' was wrong for lotus. The audit's point stands: the paper's 'alkali or alkaline earth' framing of the activation holds only for the alkali.

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F1a.definition: a stem and is a photo of the cross section of a stem
use: A lotus stem is mainly made up by the pith protected by the cortex (Figure 1a,b).
A leaf is largely composed of mesophyll tissues that produce organics utilizing photosynthesis (Figure 1b,c).

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images show both carbon materials principally inherit the morphology of the organs, which is not unexpected since pyrolysis primarily generates micropores (Figure 2a,c).
Under transmission electron microscopy (TEM), micropores and highly disordered texture in the flakes are observed (Figure 2b,d).

use: Under transmission electron microscopy (TEM), micropores and highly disordered texture in the flakes are observed (Figure 2b,d).

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F1e.definition: Concentrations of selected ions in lotus stems and leaves determined by ICP. The overall metal content is higher in stems and K is dominant
use: Indeed, the inductively coupled plasma (ICP) measurement of selected eight common metals shows the overall metal content is higher in the stems and K is dominant (Figure 1e; Table S1, Supporting Information).

Figure 3a shows the $\Nu_{2}$ adsorption–desorption isotherms of the S-carbon and L-carbon, and the derived pore size distribution calculated using density functional theory (DFT) method on the adsorption isotherm is presented in Figure 3b.

The BET surface area of the S-carbon is $\approx50\%$ higher than the L-carbon, while WS-carbon and WL-carbon have close surface area, showing the effect of ion concentration in the organs on the surface area of the derived carbon
use: Figure 3a shows the $\Nu_{2}$ adsorption–desorption isotherms of the S-carbon and L-carbon, and the derived pore size distribution calculated using density functional theory (DFT) method on the adsorption isotherm is presented in Figure 3b.

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F5d.definition: Concentrations of selected ions in celery stems and leaves determined by ICP. The overall metal content is higher in stems and K is dominant
use: Indeed, the amount of metal ions in the celery and asparagus lettuce stems are higher than in their leaves, as confirmed by ICP, and the corresponding carbon from celery and asparagus lettuce stems have higher surface area carbon than those from the leaves (Figures 5a–d and 6a–d).

The relatively high content of metal ions and especially K in the celery stem (Figure 5d; Table S1, Supporting Information) intrigue us to study the effect of pyrolyzing conditions such as temperature and time on the porosity of carbon products.

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F5e.definition: Specific surface area of the CS-carbon and the CL-carbon pyrolyzed at temperature from 800 to $1100^{\circ}{\mathrm{C}}$
use: Specific surface area up to around $2200\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ could be obtained when pyrolyzed at $1100~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $3\textrm{h}$ or at $1000~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $^{7\textrm{h}}$ (Figure 5e; Figures S9 and S10, Supporting Information).

The pyrolyzed celery leaves (CL-carbon), unexpectedly, have specific surface area less than $500~\mathrm{m}^{2}~\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ at the same pyrolyzing conditions as celery stems (CS-carbon), although their metal ions contents are not low (Figure 5e; Figure S9, Supporting Information).

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F6d.definition: Concentrations of selected ions in asparagus lettuce stems and leaves determined by ICP. The overall metal content is higher in stems and K is dominant

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F6e.definition: ${\mathsf N}_{2}$ adsorption–desorption isotherms of the AS-carbon and the AL-carbon pyrolyzed at $800^{\circ}\mathrm{C}.$

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F3c.definition: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential thermogravimetry (DTG) curves of the stems and HCl-washed stems (W-stem), showing washing could effectively leach the acid soluble organic matters in the stems
use: Figure 3c shows the thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential thermogravimetry (DTG) curves of the stems and HCl-washed stems.

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F3d.definition: Specific surface area of the S-carbon and the L-carbon pyrolyzed at temperature from 500 to $900^{\circ}{\mathsf{C}}$ , illustrating that the pore generation is largely correlated to the process of carbonaceous matter densification, rather than the decomposition process. The higher content of salts in stems than in leaves creates more porosity by the embeded salt in situ activation
use: Although $62.2\%$ weight loss takes place before $500~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $7\%$ weight loss occurs between 500 and $800~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the stems, the specific surface area of the S-carbon is only $\approx220\mathrm{m}^{2}\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ when pyrolyzed at $500~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , and the specific surface area significantly increases when the pyrolysis temperature rises to $800~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (Figure 3d).

As a result, the highly effective embedded salt activation is the cause for large surface area difference between washed and unwashed stems pyrolyzed at $800~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{~}}$ and also between S-carbon and L-carbon pyrolyzed at different temperatures (Figure 3d) and even when withered (Figure S3, Supporting Information).

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F4c.definition: The specific capacitance of the S-carbon and the L-carbon at different scan rates
use: Due to the 3D interconnected porous structure, the S-carbon can deliver $72\%$ of the capacitance even at a high scan rate of $500\mathrm{mV}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ (Figure 4c).

The L-carbon has similar capacitive behavior and cycling stability as the S-carbon (Figure S6, Supporting Information), but due to its lower specific surface, the L-carbon has lower specific capacitance than the S-carbon (Figure 4c).

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F5g.definition: The specific capacitance of the CS-carbon and the CL-carbon at different scan rate
use: The CL-carbon pyrolyzed at $800~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ has $85\%$ of the specific capacitance of CS-carbon at a scan rate of $5\mathrm{mV~s^{-1}}$ (Figure 5f,g).

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F6g.definition: The specific capacitance of the AS-carbon and the AL-carbon at different scan rate

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F4a.definition: Cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves of the S-carbon at different scan rates from 5 to $500\mathsf{m V}\mathsf{s}^{-\mathsf{T}}$
use: Almost rectangular cyclic voltammograms (CV) are presented at a scan rate from 5 to $500\mathrm{mV}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ without any redox peak (Figure 4a), and no plateau in galvanostatic charge–discharge curves at different current rates (Figure 4b), indicating the electrochemical double layer capacitive behavior and pseudocapacitance from the surface oxygen functional groups.
The specific capacitance at a scan rate of $5\mathrm{mV}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ calculated from the typical CV curve shown in Figure 4a is $174\mathrm{Fg^{-1}}$ .

10.1002/adfm.201604687#F4d.definition: Cyclic performance of the S-carbon-based symmetric supercapacitor by repeating galvanostatic charge– discharge at $1\mathsf{A}\mathsf{g}^{-\top}$
use: The S-carbon also exhibits high cycling performance, having no capacitance fading after $10~000$ charge–discharge cycles at $1\mathrm{~A~}\mathrm{~g~}^{-1}$ (Figure 4d).
